For you herdsmen,

Do not torment me; heed my words,
I beg you, give me a horse,
Accept these sorrowful words I speak.
If you deem my plea wicked,
Drag me along the road
And hand me over to the Dangyts.
If you deem my plea unjust,
Then put me to death.
If you pity a slave,
Heed what I have said;
If you count me as a human being,
Lend me the strength of one horse.
I am your captive held in bonds,
I am a slave within your hands.
I am yours to do with as you will,
I am a man in your own hands.
I am nothing but a captive slave,
Black Khan's dark-eyed son.”
When he heard these tidings,
Karagul, chief of the herdsmen—
There stood the sly wretch,
The forceful Karagul,
Who from his khan, brave Kyyaz,
Had taken his example.
Exceedingly wrathful Karagul
Grew furious and made ready;
The accursed madman
Confronted him in a rage:
“Look how this rabid, cunning slave
Has run mad!
His armor once weighed eighty-four,
Wherever he struck, red fire flared.
While the doomed man still had strength,
He was a mass of glowing embers,
He was a bullet forged of steel.
He was the Kyrgyz people's crimson banner,
And uproar among their enemies.
When he drew breath, he could burst the gall,
A silent, deadly crimson poison.
Now his poison is spent and his strength gone,
His power is exhausted and his blood drained;
All strength has left me, Külchoro.
The armored coat with golden collar and copper sleeves
Has been stripped from my back.
The host that wrought slaughter at my cry
Has been taken from Külchoro.
My flesh is but a blue scrap,
My blood no more than a spoonful;
I have no voice with which to shout,
No fistful of hair left to bristle,
No tongue with which to speak.
Accursed world, ever stalking me with disaster!
I have no waist on which to bind my belt,
No refuge where I may stand firm,
No dark, rugged mountain,
No black cliff to circle,
No mountain on which to lean,
No strength with which to strike,
No power left to fight.
Once we brought the whole world to heel
And dealt doom to all we met—
In former days we were heroes.
Now cut off from the living,
Our shoulders gouged on either side,
We gather firewood as slaves,
Unslain, we live as captives,
Poor wretches wandering astray.
Let the lord show mercy—
That is why we beg for a mount.
If your valor is true,
You will heed these words
And lend me the strength of one horse.
The Argyn Kyrgyz rode forth,
Intent on slaughtering heroes.
Many a bride and many a maiden
They kept unmarried for many years;
Those who met them were laid low,
And noble heads were crushed.
For mortal folk until doomsday,
It became a deed never to be forgotten.
You ravaged the borders by force;
Though Kyrgyz by birth,
You wore the crimson collar.
You did a deed worse than any Chinese warrior.
Your forefathers were enemies by nature,
And you were born of Almambet.
You raised great tumult and uproar
And committed an exceptionally evil deed.
You cut down those who fled,
And did a deed never to leave our hearts;
You struck down all you met,
And felled all who crossed you.
You bloodied those who encountered you,
And slew all who came your way.
You broke my back many times,
And slaughtered still more of my people.
When the great host of black-clad Jediger
Swept forward, you drove it back;
You destroyed the leaders of the people
And parted us from our dear ones.
You bent and broke my back,
And swept away my warriors.
You scattered many brains,
And made slaves of my renowned men;
You tore open my throat and made it a road,
Slaughtered and disgraced my people,
And utterly destroyed my ancient line.
You turned summer into autumn
And laid my joyful ones in the dust;
Now you have fallen into my hands
And been caught in my iron net.
Though you lament, I shall not hear your plea.
His lashes are flame and his eyes are embers;
No man is so accursed as he.
Yesterday Chynkojo, son of Shygai—
A formidable lord in all he did—
Ravaged and slaughtered,
Killing my lionhearted hero Chynkojo;
Like a fire extinguished, he destroyed
My brave warrior Toltoy,
Who had broken my back so many times.
He cut down my mighty host.
He began a terrible conflict,
Leaving sixty women widowed,
And their villages desolate;
The women wept in widowhood,
Their children enslaved as spoils—
Thus he broke my back
And left many of my heroes in pain.
He extinguished the fire that burned,
And plundered all the Jediger
Who filled the Seven Valleys, driving them away.
He cut down those who challenged him,
And devoured all he encountered;
He brought those who fought him to ruin
And crushed all who crossed his path.
He ravaged Afghanistan and withdrew,
And set the Jediger aflame.
Orphans wailed, sons were left behind,
And slender-waisted women in crimson gowns
Were left trembling as widows.
Giants were broken and laid low,
And every valiant warrior left on foot.
He slaughtered countless elders,
And utterly destroyed all I possessed,
Making your Jediger blood
Flow like the waters of a river.
He ruined your homeland and left it bereaved,
And took every able-bodied son
As a captive household slave.
He chose the finest steeds and took them,
Though we were once kinsmen by birth.
From the horses left desolate,
Take whichever lets itself be caught and ride.
Keep your word and return;
You reeking, stinking slave,
Do not stray from anything I have said!”
Saying this, Karagul
Unleashed his wrath.
Külchoro, favored by fortune,
Was struck by bitter misfortune;
The noble hero who once rode chargers
Now grieved, unable even to find a mare.
As he turned back,
Tears streamed from his two eyes
And fell down his breast.
His joints weakened as evening fell;
Sobbing bitterly, longing to die,
His two eyes strained in desperation.
